A lot of these predictions are built upon Ray Kurzweil, but I think he's increasingly just accelerating all his predictions to stave off his own mortality. I don't think it's a coincidence that he puts the time for the advent of the era such that technology would be adding more than 1 year of life expectancy per year (or in other words, effective immortality) in the 2030s. That's exactly when he'd be hitting his 80s and starting to reach his expected expiration date.

Is it even advanced medical technology which has been primarily responsible for so greatly extending the average life? Look back at 'ye olde times' and you'll often find the well to do lived just as long then as they do today. I mean you can go quite far back. Pythagoras, born 570BC, died at age 75 for instance. The thing that separated them from the proletariat was an abundance of clean food, good hygiene, no obligation to military duty, and the means to leave areas when military conflict was arising. The first of those issues the poor of today have relatively good access to, and the military stuff is now a relatively nonissue in developed nations - not only because most won't see service but even those that do won't often die because of it.

So I think the strict interpretation of linking increased longevity solely to increased medical technology is simply wrong. And like with many things there's no reason to believe that we're on a strictly exponential curve, and not a sigmoid curve instead. Space is a good example there. In the 60s people probably thought by now we'd be flying between the planets and even starting to send expeditions to distant solar systems. Instead once the government funding fell off, space as an industry basically died for the next 50 years.

That said, pragmatic views are time and again proven to be wrong when it comes to trying to predict the future now a days. Kurzweil has a great track record and I certainly hope he's right, but I fear he's lost his objectivity.
